hook.text: A high-strength steel bolt snaps without warning — hydrogen atoms migrated to the stressed zone and cracked it.

buildup.text: Hydrogen embrittlement occurs when atomic hydrogen diffuses into steel and reduces ductility and toughness.

discovery.text: Hydrogen atoms are tiny enough to diffuse through the steel lattice and collect at stress concentrations.

twist.text: Higher-strength steels are more susceptible — the very property we want makes them more vulnerable.

climax.text: Hydrogen economy infrastructure — pipelines and storage tanks — must use embrittlement-resistant alloys.

punchline.text: The smallest atom causes the biggest failures in the strongest steels.

quiz.question: Why are higher-strength steels more susceptible to hydrogen embrittlement?
options: Their microstructure provides more trapping sites and higher stress concentrations
They are always used at higher temperatures
